blocks.text: The purpose of brackets in journalism

When you see brackets in a news article, it means the journalist added information. You might see a pronoun replaced with a name, like [the mayor], to clarify who a speaker meant. You might see a missing verb or a date added to make a sentence readable. Brackets protect the integrity of a quote. They show the reader exactly what the speaker said versus what the reporter added to make sense of the situation. Without brackets, a quote might be confusing or misleading. Using them correctly is a core skill for any professional writer.

Formatting is rarely the reason people enter journalism. Yet, it consumes a large portion of the day. You have to manage font sizes, citation styles, and figure placement for every story. Requirements change by publication. One editor wants AP style, another wants a specific house style. This inconsistency leads to desk rejections. You spend time fixing layouts instead of reporting. This is a primary driver of administrative burden. It adds to the 48.9 hours per week many journalists already work. It is a source of frustration that builds up over time.

You can manage formatting without buying expensive software. Start by creating a checklist for your specific publication. Include font, spacing, and citation requirements. Review this list before you submit your draft. Standardize your templates early. If you use Word or Google Docs, create a template file with your styles pre-set. This prevents the need for manual adjustments at the end of a project. Separate your writing phase from your formatting phase. Draft in a plain text editor to avoid distractions. Only move to a layout-heavy app when the text is finalized.

faq.question: Why do journalists use brackets instead of just changing the quote?
faq.answer: Changing a direct quote is unethical. Brackets show the reader that the journalist added context without altering the original speaker's words.

faq.question: How can I stop spending so much time on formatting?
faq.answer: Use templates. Set up your document styles once and reuse them. Also, keep a checklist to avoid common errors that lead to rejections.
